blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.

blocks.en:
Executable repository-level benchmarks have increasingly become a central testbed for
software engineering agents. SWE-bench and its variants pair a
natural-language issue with a repository state and an executable test
oracle, enabling standardized, verifiable evaluation of generated
patches ( Jimenez et al. 2023 ; Zan et al. 2025 ; Deng et al. 2025 ) . Most benchmarks,
however, retain a single issue or pull request (PR) as the basic task
unit. This abstraction captures isolated bug fixes and localized features,
but only a restricted portion of real software development. In practice,
a single feature, migration, dependency upgrade, or systematic fix often evolves across
multiple PRs. These changes may be sequential, branch in parallel, or
converge through later integration. The missing abstraction is therefore
not merely longer context or a larger patch, but the dependency
structure connecting multiple changes into a coherent engineering
objective. Figure 1 summarizes this mismatch
between dependency-structured development, proxy-based task construction,
and structure-agnostic credit assignment.

blocks.en:
Recent work has moved beyond isolated PRs by grouping changes through
release windows, temporal spans, explicit cross-references, or object-level
dependencies ( Thai et al. 2025 ; Chen et al. 2026 ; Jiang et al. 2026 ; Zhou et al. 2026 ) . These efforts advance long-horizon
software engineering, yet two coupled challenges remain. First, these aggregation signals are imperfect proxies
for task coherence: temporal proximity can merge unrelated changes,
explicit references are sparse, and coarse overlap is often dominated by
frequently modified utilities, configuration files, or dependency
manifests. Moreover, a related change set does not itself define a
reproducible task with a valid base state, task specification, and
executable oracle. Second, current evaluation poorly captures structured
partial progress. Binary resolution ignores progress on unsolved tasks,
while flat test- or PR-level aggregation overlooks dependencies and may
over-credit downstream behavior built on incomplete upstream changes. The
same issue weakens reinforcement learning: binary rewards are sparse,
whereas patch-similarity and learned rewards may not align with executable
task semantics ( Tao et al. 2025 ; Wei et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026 ; Shum et al. 2025 ) . Addressing these limitations requires a unified,
code-grounded representation for executable task construction,
dependency-aware evaluation, and verifiable learning signals.

blocks.en:
We introduce WEAVE , a framework for weaving real-world code
evolution into executable, dependency-structured tasks for benchmarking
and training code agents. As illustrated in
Figure 1 , WEAVE starts from verified
atomic PRs, identifies code-grounded relations through typed change loci
calibrated by repository-local frequencies, and organizes related changes
into bounded dependency DAGs. Each DAG is instantiated as a reproducible
repository-level task with a unified specification and executable oracle,
while remaining evaluator-side metadata unavailable to the agent. Beyond
task construction, the DAG provides a common interface for measuring and
learning from structured progress. We introduce Graph Credit, a
deterministic and test-grounded metric that complements binary resolution
by rewarding dependency-consistent partial completion. The same structure
supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning, while the
constructed corpus provides long-horizon trajectories for supervised
fine-tuning. WEAVE thereby unifies executable task construction,
structure-aware evaluation, and agent training over realistic multi-PR
software evolution.

blocks.en:
To assess both the benchmarking and training utility of WEAVE ,
we conduct a four-part empirical study covering task construction, agent
evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. WEAVE yields 3200 training tasks and
300 held-out benchmark tasks spanning
six programming languages. Its code-grounded aggregation
produces more coherent task groupings and a higher executable-task yield
than temporal and coarse-overlap baselines. Evaluations of
eight software engineering agents further show that Graph Credit
exposes structurally inconsistent credit obscured by flat scoring. Under
matched supervised-token budgets, WEAVE -based supervision
improves downstream agent performance, while graph-structured rewards
outperform binary and flat-reward baselines. Together, these results
establish dependency-structured tasks as a principled foundation for both
evaluating and improving code agents.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are threefold: • Executable dependency-structured task construction. We introduce WEAVE , a framework that constructs bounded
dependency DAGs from verified PR histories using
repository-calibrated typed change loci, and instantiates each graph
as a unified executable task. • Structure-aware evaluation and verifiable credit. We introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric for
evaluating dependency-consistent partial progress. By conditioning
credit on upstream resolution, it complements binary and flat scoring
while providing a dense, verifiable signal for agent optimization. • Empirical validation for benchmarking and training. Extensive experiments show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, captures progress missed by structure-agnostic evaluation, and
provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.

blocks.en: 2.1 Single-PR Software Engineering Benchmarks
blocks.zh: 2.1 单一PR软件工程基准

blocks.en:
SWE-bench established executable repository-level evaluation by pairing
an issue and a pre-change repository state with F2P/P2P tests ( Jimenez et al. 2023 ) . Subsequent benchmarks improve instance
quality or expand the same atomic issue–PR formulation across visual
software, programming languages, recent repository states, and more
challenging enterprise-scale changes ( Jimenez et al. 2023 ; Yang et al. 2024 ; Zan et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025a ; Deng et al. 2025 ) . Executable workbenches such
as SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-Smith, and SWE-rebench V2 further scale this
primitive for trajectory generation and model training ( Pan et al. 2024 ; Jain et al. 2025 ; Yang et al. 2025 ; Badertdinov et al. 2025 ) .
Together with recent contamination analyses, these works establish the foundations of
verifiable SWE-agent evaluation and training, while generally retaining
an individual issue, commit, or PR as the basic task unit.

blocks.en:
Recent work extends software-engineering evaluation to broader units by
aggregating changes across releases, features, or development roadmaps ( Thai et al. 2025 ; Zhou et al. 2026 ; Xu et al. 2026 ) , or by
preserving repository evolution through temporal PR ranges, commit spans,
release chains, and chronologically linked fixes ( Shastry et al. 2026 ; Chen et al. 2026 ; Lam et al. 2026 ; Jin et al. 2026 ) . Other approaches reconstruct milestone DAGs or mine
explicitly referenced PR chains ( Deng et al. 2026 ; Jiang et al. 2026 ) . These benchmarks commonly
measure progress through flat test completion, stage- or component-level
scores, or milestone resolution. Related work has also explored denser
signals based on patch similarity, weighted tests, learned reward models,
process feedback, enhanced test oracles, and multidimensional evaluation ( Wei et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026 ; Shum et al. 2025 ; Dai et al. 2024 ; Yu et al. 2025 ; Tao et al. 2025 ; He et al. 2025 ; Miserendino et al. 2025 ) , while graph
structures and cross-language code representations have been used to
organize agent workflows or support structural program analysis ( Chen et al. 2024 ; Song et al. 2024 ; Zhang et al. 2025b ; Vogel et al. 2026 ) . WEAVE complements these directions by constructing executable
PR-DAG tasks from repository-calibrated code coupling and deriving
graph-conditioned partial credit from node-attributed tests, which can
also serve as a dense, verifiable outcome signal during optimization.

validated atomic PR instances. As illustrated in
Figure 2 , the construction contains two stages.

modifies and aggregates strongly coupled PRs into bounded dependency

as a single-environment task with a unified specification, executable
tests, and node-level test attribution. The resulting graph is retained
as evaluator-side metadata and is subsequently used for the
graph-conditioned credit and reinforcement-learning methods in
Section 4 .

blocks.zh: 3.2 仓库 -- -- 分析的DAG 建筑业

blocks.en:
Temporal proximity and file-level overlap are insufficient for reliable
dependency recovery: nearby PRs may be unrelated, while frequently
modified files may connect otherwise independent changes. WEAVE therefore represents PRs at the level of typed change loci and calibrates
their shared evidence against repository-specific modification patterns.

blocks.en:
To validate WEAVE ’s construction pipeline, we evaluate whether
typed-locus coupling recovers true dependency edges more reliably than
single-signal alternatives. The evaluation covers 30 repositories
containing 1,198 validated atomic PRs. To establish ground truth,
three expert annotators independently assess candidate PR pairs and
label each as dependency , same-task but independent , loosely related , or unrelated ; a senior annotator
adjudicates disagreements, yielding 219 gold dependency edges
(Fleiss’ κ \kappa = 0.791). Each method produces a scored ranking of
candidate edges; we report macro-averaged AP over repositories,
Coverage—the fraction of gold edges recalled at full emission—and
pooled Precision at rank 50 (P@50). All methods feed into the identical
downstream executable construction pipeline (§ 3.3 ).

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
This paper addresses a fundamental limitation of current software
engineering agent evaluation: the lack of a task abstraction that captures
causal dependencies among multiple repository changes. We introduce WEAVE , which recovers dependency DAGs from verified PR histories
through repository-calibrated typed-locus coupling. The same graph
representation unifies task construction, dependency-conditioned
partial credit (Graph Credit), and structured reward design, enabling
consistent evaluation and optimization of long-horizon code agents.
Experiments across construction quality, agent benchmarking, supervised
training, and reinforcement learning demonstrate the effectiveness of WEAVE as both a challenging evaluation workbench and an
effective substrate for improving code agents.

blocks.en: A.1 Typed Change Loci Extraction

blocks.en:
Recovering dependency structure from PR histories requires a
representation granular enough to distinguish genuine engineering
dependencies from coincidental co-modification. File-level
overlap—the most common proxy in prior work—conflates distinct
changes within shared files and over-connects PRs that modify
frequently touched configuration manifests, barrel imports, or
dependency lockfiles. WEAVE addresses this by representing
each PR as a set of typed change loci : fine-grained program
entities extracted from its code diff, each annotated with a structural
category that determines its evidential role in coupling computation.
We define five locus types, each designed to capture a distinct channel
of cross-PR evidence:

Function, method, and class definitions identified via

resolution. This captures entities that do not correspond to

JSON, and INI configuration files; database migration column

(e.g., server.http.timeout ). 4. Declarations and signatures ( ℒ decl \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decl}} ): Type signatures, interface
definitions, abstract method declarations, and trait/protocol

blocks.en:
We generate with GLM-5.2 rather than the strongest evaluated
configuration (Claude Opus 4.7 + Cline, per the RQ2 results in the main
text) for three reasons. First, GLM-5.2 has openly released weights, so the
resulting corpus can be published without the derived-data restrictions
that proprietary model outputs carry, and the generation stage is
self-hostable and therefore independently reproducible. Second, GLM-5.2
is the second-strongest configuration on WEAVE-Bench (43.0% versus 48.7% Resolved); the best-of-3 protocol absorbs most of
this 5.7 pp gap at the corpus level. Third, generator and student share
a broadly similar tool-invocation format, which reduces format
adaptation during distillation. The cost is throughput: GLM-5.2 averages
138.2 turns and 7.52 M cumulative tokens per benchmark task, against
46.8 turns and 2.11 M for Claude Opus 4.7. This 3.6 × \times generation
overhead is why we cap attempts at three per task rather than sampling
more widely.

computed only on assistant-generated tokens; tool results, file
contents, and test output are supplied as context but excluded from the

truncated during training; training at this length uses sequence
parallelism. Learning rate : with only 2,304 trajectories, the
corpus is small enough that the higher end of the search range
overfits within one epoch. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B activates roughly 3B
parameters per token, so its optimal rate is close to—though slightly

GRPO is critic-free: for each task we sample G = 8 G=8 rollouts, score each
with R WEAVE R_{\mathrm{WEAVE}} , and take the advantage of a rollout to be its
reward centered and scaled by the mean and standard deviation within its own group . No value network, and hence no generalized
advantage estimation, is used. Group-relative normalization makes the
gradient invariant to task difficulty, so that easy and hard tasks
contribute comparably.

blocks.en:
Group-relative normalization also explains why reward density matters
here beyond the usual sparse-reward argument: a group whose G G rollouts
all receive the same reward contributes no gradient at all, so a sparse
reward wastes rollout budget outright rather than merely learning
slowly. Because Graph Credit is continuous and dependency-conditioned,
its groups almost always exhibit within-group spread. The empirical
consequence is quantified in § D.3 .

集团关系正常化也解释了奖励密度问题的原因。
在这里,除了通常的微薄的回报:一个GG推出的团体
都得到同样的奖励 根本没有梯度,所以很少

慢慢来。 因为图信用是连续的 依赖条件,

后果在D.3节中量化。
